references.text: The glory of the Lord appeared in the cloud, as a direct fulfillment of the promise that they would see the glory of the Lord.
Israel's earlier grumbling against Moses and Aaron at the Red Sea shows a pattern of complaining against leaders.
The glory of the Lord was revealed to the assembly in response to the people's grumbling, a similar pattern to what happened in the wilderness.
Moses asks why the people are grumbling against him and points out that their complaint is really against the Lord.
The people argue with Moses and grumble again, and Moses points out that they are testing the Lord.
The glory of the Lord is a central theme when God reveals Himself to Moses.
The glory of the Lord will be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together—a prophetic parallel.
Paul warns against grumbling as the Israelites did in the wilderness, pointing to the consequences of their complaints.
The exhortation to do everything without grumbling or doubt stands in contrast to Israel's behavior in the wilderness.
Connects the concept of 'the glory of the Lord' in the context of human challenge and the expectation to see it.
Highlights the theology that God's judgment can be averted through obedience and repentance.
Contrasts the people's denial of their own harsh words against God and His servants.
Compares the prophecy about seeing the glory of the Lord with the historical experience at Horeb.
Contrasts how God 'hears' both the people's complaints and a king's humility.
Highlights the theology that today's actions directly determine tomorrow's consequences.
Compares the situation where the Lord's wrath is declared with the hope that prayer can avert it.
Describes the same event (the meat miracle) and confirms that the people wept before the Lord's ears.
Contrasts God's hearing of the people's complaints with Moses' intercession.
